Text: The first truly international measurement standard was the {{c1::meter::unit}}, established by the {{c2::French Academy of Sciences::institution}} in the {{c3::1790s::decade}}.
Back Extra:
Why: a platinum rod was made to represent the chosen length — a physical object to define the meter.

Cue: one meter is, very roughly, nose to fingertip with your arm and hand stretched out horizontally.

Text: The standard meter was originally chosen to be one {{c1::ten-millionth::fraction}} of the distance from the Earth's {{c2::equator to either pole::from where to where}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the span runs equator → pole (either one), not pole to pole.

Ex: modern measurements of the Earth show the intended length was off by only about one-fiftieth of 1%.

Text: Since 1983, the meter is defined as the length of the path traveled by {{c1::light in vacuum}} during {{c2::1/299,792,458}} of a second.
Back Extra:
Cue: the fraction is the reciprocal of the speed of light — 299,792,458 m/s was its best measured value under the old meter definition.

Pathway: Earth's equator-to-pole quadrant (1790s) → engraved marks on a platinum-iridium bar (1889) → krypton-86 wavelengths (1960) → light travel time (1983, current).

Text: The standard unit of time is the {{c1::second}}, now defined in terms of the frequency of radiation emitted by {{c2::cesium::element}} atoms when they pass between two particular states.
Back Extra:
Ex: one second is defined as the time for 9,192,631,770 oscillations of the cesium radiation.

Distinguish: the OLD definition was 1/86,400 of a mean solar day (24 h × 60 min × 60 s = 86,400 s).

Text: The standard unit of mass is the {{c1::kilogram}} — defined as exactly the mass of a particular {{c2::platinum-iridium::alloy}} cylinder kept at the {{c3::International Bureau of Weights and Measures::institution}} near Paris.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: same alloy, different object — the 1889 meter standard was a platinum-iridium BAR with engraved marks; the mass standard is a platinum-iridium CYLINDER.

Ex: for practical purposes, 1 kg weighs about 2.2 pounds on Earth.

Text: When dealing with atoms and molecules, mass is usually given in the {{c1::unified atomic mass unit (u or amu)}} rather than in kilograms.
Back Extra:
Ex: 1 u = 1.6605 × 10^-27 kg.

Why: atomic-scale masses are absurdly small in kilograms — a proton is about 10^-27 kg — so a matched unit is handier.
verified_by: agent, read from page render this run

Text: In the metric system, larger and smaller units are defined in multiples of {{c1::10::number}} from the standard unit, which makes calculation particularly easy.
Back Extra:
Ex: 1 kilometer = 1000 m; 1 centimeter = 1/100 m; 1 millimeter = 1/1000 m.

Why: the prefixes attach to any unit, not just length — a centiliter is 1/100 liter, and a kilogram is 1000 grams.

Text: The SI prefix micro is abbreviated {{c1::μ (mu)::symbol}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the Latin letter m already belongs to milli — micro takes the Greek letter mu instead.

Ex: 1 μg (microgram), 1 μm (micrometer).

Text: The SI prefix deka is abbreviated {{c1::da::symbol}} — the only two-letter SI prefix abbreviation.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the plain letter d already belongs to deci — deka gets "da".

Ex: a dekameter is abbreviated dam.

Text: SI prefix abbreviations are {{c1::uppercase::uppercase/lowercase}} for mega (10^6) and larger, and {{c1::lowercase::uppercase/lowercase}} for kilo (10^3) and smaller.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: case is load-bearing — M (mega) and m (milli) name wildly different sizes.

Cue: big multipliers, big letters.

Text: In measurement, a unit is {{c1::the named amount a measurement is expressed in}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "The measurement of any quantity is made relative to a particular standard or unit, and this unit must be specified along with the numerical value of the quantity."

Distinguish: the unit is what you express results in (meters); the standard is the agreed physical reference that defines the unit exactly.

Text: In measurement, a standard is {{c1::the agreed physical reference defining a unit exactly}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "The measurement of any quantity is made relative to a particular standard or unit, and this unit must be specified along with the numerical value of the quantity."

Distinguish: the standard is the defining reference itself (the platinum-iridium kilogram cylinder near Paris); the unit is the named amount you measure in (the kilogram).

Text: A base quantity is {{c1::one defined by its own standard, not other quantities}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Physical quantities can be divided into two categories: base quantities and derived quantities."

Distinguish: a derived quantity (like speed) is built from base quantities; a base quantity rests directly on a standard.

Why: scientists want the smallest set that fully describes the physical world — in the SI it turns out to be seven.
verified_by: long-blank warning cleared: 9 plain words is the floor that keeps the mandated discriminator (defined by its OWN standard, not from other quantities)

Text: Derived quantities are {{c1::quantities defined in terms of the base quantities}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "All other quantities can be defined in terms of these seven base quantities, and hence are referred to as derived quantities."

Distinguish: a base quantity is defined by its own standard; a derived one is built from base quantities — e.g., speed = distance ÷ time.

Text: An operational definition is {{c1::a definition that specifies a rule or procedure}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "To define any quantity, whether base or derived, we can specify a rule or procedure, and this is called an operational definition."

Parts: operational — from "operation": the definition tells you which operations (steps) to carry out.
